title: Cache-Aside Has a Contract
hook: A cache hit is useful only if the returned value is allowed to be stale.
premise: The database remains authoritative. Define the key, freshness window, miss behavior, and update policy before adding a cache to a read path.
roadmap: Choose eligible reads
Cache repeatable reads whose freshness and authorization requirements are understood.
Design the key
Include tenant, resource version, and relevant query context without leaking private data.
Bound the lifetime
Set expiry from the product's freshness contract rather than an arbitrary default.
Handle cache misses
Load from the source with bounded concurrency and a clear failure path.
Coordinate updates
Invalidate or replace cached state according to an explicitly tested write policy.
Test cache loss
Verify the source survives cold starts and cache unavailability.
decisions: Cache-aside
Use cache-aside when the application can manage misses and freshness deliberately.
Concurrent misses and write races can expose stale data or overload the source.
Read-through abstraction
Use a shared abstraction when consistent loading rules reduce duplicated application code.
The abstraction must still expose timeouts, freshness, and failure behavior.
No cache
Keep direct reads when the source is fast enough or correctness requires immediate freshness.
Avoiding a cache can simplify operations, but does not remove the need to measure source capacity.
incident: Notice inconsistent reads
Different requests return different versions of the same logical object.
Inspect key dimensions
Check tenant, filters, version, and serialization behavior in the cache key.
Compare authoritative state
Determine whether the cache or source contains the correct current value.
Bypass narrowly
Route only the affected class to the source while protecting database capacity.
Repair update semantics
Fix the invalidation or write-order race rather than only flushing everything.
Test concurrent changes
Exercise read misses racing with updates and delayed cache writes.
metrics: Hit ratio by workload
Measure hits for specific useful request classes rather than one global percentage.
A high hit ratio can hide a small expensive miss path or incorrect cached responses.
Stale-read age
Measure the age or version gap of cached data against the accepted freshness window.
Expiry time is not always the same as data age when values are repopulated from stale sources.
Source fallback load
Track database demand during misses, cold starts, and cache failures.
A cache can make steady state cheap while making recovery unexpectedly dangerous.
lab: Define freshness
Create a local record whose acceptable stale-read interval is explicit.
Implement scoped keys
Include tenant and resource identity in each cache lookup.
Update during a miss
Pause a source read while another client writes a newer value.
Resume the old read
Observe whether it repopulates an obsolete cache entry.
Apply a repair policy
Test version-aware writes or another policy appropriate to the contract.
Remove the cache
Verify bounded fallback and correct responses during complete cache loss.
takeaway: Caching changes correctness and recovery behavior, not only latency.

title: Invalidation Is Delivery Work
hook: A missed invalidation event can turn a fast cache into a long-lived lie.
premise: Distinguish expiry, explicit invalidation, and event-driven refresh. Delivery and ordering guarantees depend on the chosen transport.
roadmap: State the freshness bound
Identify which stale responses are acceptable and for how long.
Name the changed entity
Publish stable resource identities and versions instead of ambiguous delete-all messages.
Choose delivery semantics
Use a transport whose loss and replay behavior matches the consistency requirement.
Handle reordered updates
Prevent an older refresh from overwriting a newer cached version.
Keep a recovery path
Use expiry or reconciliation to recover from missed notifications.
Test disconnected consumers
Verify behavior when an invalidator is offline during writes.
decisions: TTL-only expiry
Use expiry when a bounded stale window is acceptable and simple operation is valuable.
A short TTL increases source load; a long TTL increases stale exposure.
Best-effort notifications
Use transient notifications only when loss is tolerable or another mechanism repairs it.
Redis Pub/Sub-style notifications are not a durable event log for disconnected consumers.
Durable change stream
Use durable events when consumers must recover missed changes.
Offsets, retention, schema evolution, and duplicate handling become part of cache maintenance.
incident: Find a stale cohort
Only some cache nodes continue serving a removed or changed record.
Check delivery gaps
Compare consumer connection history with the source update timeline.
Inspect version ordering
Look for an old refresh that arrived after a newer invalidation.
Repair affected keys
Refresh or evict the known identities without creating an uncontrolled source surge.
Restore replay or expiry
Ensure missed changes have a bounded recovery mechanism.
Test disconnect recovery
Write during a consumer outage and verify eventual convergence after restart.
metrics: Invalidation delay
Measure source-commit-to-cache-convergence time for relevant entity classes.
Publisher success alone does not prove every cache consumer applied the change.
Version regressions
Count attempted writes of older versions over newer cache entries.
Out-of-order delivery can occur even when individual workers process events sequentially.
Repair volume
Track keys refreshed by expiry or reconciliation after delivery gaps.
A growing repair burden may reveal an unreliable primary invalidation path.
lab: Create two cache consumers
Use a local source and two independently updated cache views.
Disconnect one consumer
Apply several source changes while one invalidator is offline.
Reconnect and compare
Measure stale versions before replay, expiry, or reconciliation.
Reorder two events
Deliver an older refresh after a newer update.
Protect the version
Reject stale overwrites using the selected version contract.
Verify bounded staleness
Document the worst observed recovery interval under each delivery mode.
takeaway: An invalidation signal needs a loss, ordering, and recovery story.

title: Stop the Cache Stampede
hook: One expired hot key can send thousands of identical reads to your database.
premise: A popular value expires while many requests arrive together. Protect the source and define whether serving an older value is allowed.
roadmap: Identify hot expirations
Measure miss bursts by key class and source request amplification.
Coalesce concurrent loads
Let one loader refresh a key while other requests share or await the result.
Bound the wait
Apply timeouts and cancellation to requests waiting for a refresh.
Consider stale serving
Serve a bounded stale value only when the product contract permits it.
Spread refresh timing
Use jitter or early refresh to avoid synchronized expiry waves.
Test loader failure
Ensure a crashed refresher does not leave the key permanently unavailable.
decisions: Single-flight loading
Use in-process coalescing when one node receives many requests for the same missing value.
Other nodes can still stampede; the scope of coalescing must match the workload.
Distributed refresh lease
Use a bounded shared lease when refresh coordination spans nodes.
Lease ownership, expiry, and safe release need careful handling during pauses and crashes.
Stale-while-revalidate
Use bounded stale serving for data whose correctness contract permits it.
Do not serve revoked permissions or other freshness-critical data merely to preserve availability.
incident: Observe the miss burst
Database demand spikes immediately after a popular cache entry expires.
Confirm duplicated loads
Correlate source queries with the same logical cache key.
Bound source access
Limit concurrent refreshes and shed excess work if necessary.
Restore one safe value
Warm the key or permit bounded stale serving only when authorized by the contract.
Fix refresh coordination
Add coalescing and a failure-safe refresh lifecycle.
Replay synchronized expiry
Expire the hot key under controlled concurrent load and measure amplification.
metrics: Loads per miss wave
Count source loads triggered by one logical missing-key interval.
A good aggregate hit ratio can still hide a devastating periodic stampede.
Refresh wait time
Measure how long followers wait for the elected loader.
Coalescing can turn source overload into a long wait unless deadlines remain bounded.
Stale responses served
Count responses served from an intentionally stale value and their age.
Stale serving is a product trade-off that must be visible, not a hidden fallback.
lab: Create a slow source
Serve one synthetic expensive value behind a short-lived cache entry.
Synchronize clients
Release many local clients just after the entry expires.
Count source calls
Record how many duplicate loads the naive implementation issues.
Add coalescing
Share one bounded load result across concurrent requests.
Crash the loader
Verify that waiting requests recover or fail clearly when refresh fails.
Compare the tail
Measure source amplification, waiting time, errors, and stale exposure together.
takeaway: Protect the source during misses; a cache is most dangerous when it suddenly stops helping.

title: Hot Keys Break Even Clusters
hook: Adding cache nodes will not split one extremely popular key automatically.
premise: Distinguish a hot read, a hot mutable counter, and a large value. Their scaling and correctness constraints are different.
roadmap: Measure key concentration
Identify the fraction of demand reaching the busiest key classes.
Separate reads and writes
Determine whether the hotspot is immutable reads, mutations, or serialization of a large payload.
Replicate safe reads
Use local copies or additional read paths only when freshness permits them.
Partition mutable work
Shard counters or state only with an explicit aggregation and consistency contract.
Bound payload cost
Reduce unnecessary fields and measure transfer and deserialization overhead.
Test skew explicitly
Benchmark the observed popularity distribution, not only uniform random keys.
decisions: Local read cache
Use local caching for highly repeated reads with acceptable bounded staleness.
Every process needs invalidation or expiry, and cold starts can synchronize source demand.
Replicated hot value
Use multiple readable copies when the storage system and freshness contract support them.
Writes and invalidation must reach the right copies without exposing inconsistent security state.
Sharded counter
Use partitioned counters when approximate or delayed aggregation is acceptable.
A global exact check may reintroduce coordination and remove the expected scaling gain.
incident: Find one saturated node
Cluster averages look low while a node serving a hot key is overloaded.
Inspect key distribution
Measure popularity and value size without logging private key contents.
Reduce avoidable demand
Coalesce repeated work and apply targeted admission where appropriate.
Choose a semantic fix
Use replication for safe reads or a justified partitioned write design.
Check consistency cost
Verify that the change preserves freshness and business invariants.
Replay realistic skew
Compare tail latency under the same hot-key distribution.
metrics: Top-key concentration
Measure the share of traffic handled by the busiest bounded key classes.
Uniform storage size says little about the distribution of request demand.
Value transfer cost
Track payload bytes and serialization time for frequently read values.
A key can be hot because it is large, not only because it is requested often.
Per-node saturation
Compare CPU, network, and latency across cache nodes.
A healthy cluster average can conceal one node limiting the whole user journey.
lab: Seed a skewed workload
Make one synthetic key receive most requests while others remain cold.
Add a cache node
Observe whether the existing key's demand actually redistributes.
Try read replication
Test local or replicated reads with an explicit freshness window.
Try a mutable counter
Compare exact coordination with partitioned updates and later aggregation.
Measure the trade-offs
Record latency, update cost, stale age, and aggregate error where relevant.
Document the semantics
State which guarantee changed instead of describing every approach as equivalent.
takeaway: Hot-key fixes depend on what the key means, not just where it is stored.

title: Cache Memory Is a Budget
hook: A cache can run out of memory even when every key has a TTL.
premise: Expiry limits lifetime, not instantaneous demand. Account for value sizes, metadata, replication buffers, and eviction policy.
roadmap: Measure real entry cost
Include key, value, encoding, and allocator overhead in representative measurements.
Set a memory ceiling
Choose a safe limit below the host's total capacity, leaving room for non-cache overhead.
Choose eviction semantics
Match the policy to eligible keys and the cost of evicting them.
Control large values
Bound object sizes and avoid caching data whose transfer cost outweighs the benefit.
Watch churn
Measure eviction and refill rates that can turn the cache into expensive pass-through storage.
Test pressure and restart
Exercise cold starts, persistence behavior, and source protection under memory pressure.
decisions: Evict least-used data
Use a supported eviction policy when losing cached values is acceptable.
Eviction must not silently remove state that the application wrongly treats as durable authority.
Reject new writes
Use explicit rejection when eviction would violate the role of the stored data.
Clients must handle write rejection without endless retries or inconsistent fallback state.
Split cache workloads
Separate durable coordination or session needs from disposable read caching when policies differ.
More clusters add cost and operations, so split by real semantic boundaries.
incident: Notice eviction churn
Hit rate falls while writes, evictions, and source reads rise together.
Inspect entry distribution
Find oversized values, unexpected cardinality, and keys without intended expiry.
Bound new admissions
Reduce unnecessary caching while preserving essential application behavior.
Check eviction policy
Verify the configured policy matches the key population and memory role.
Repair the working set
Adjust key design, value size, or capacity based on measured reuse.
Test a cold restart
Confirm the authoritative source survives rebuilding the useful cache population.
metrics: Memory per useful entry
Measure actual memory relative to entries that produce meaningful hits.
Serialized payload bytes exclude allocator and metadata overhead.
Eviction rate
Track evictions and refills together to identify destructive churn.
Some eviction is normal; repeated eviction of hot data can erase the benefit of caching.
Source amplification
Compare source traffic before and during cache pressure.
A memory incident can become a database incident if fallback is unbounded.
lab: Set a small memory limit
Use a disposable cache with a documented eviction policy.
Mix value sizes
Load synthetic small and large entries with known access frequencies.
Exceed the working set
Observe memory, eviction, misses, and source demand.
Separate durable state
Verify critical coordination data is not silently treated as disposable cache content.
Change admission rules
Avoid storing low-reuse oversized values and compare effective hit rates.
Verify pressure behavior
Assert bounded errors and source load when the memory ceiling is reached.
takeaway: TTL, admission, eviction, and fallback together define the cache's real memory behavior.

title: Ordering Lives in a Partition
hook: A globally ordered story can become several locally ordered event streams.
premise: For a partitioned log, identify which entity requires ordering and how its events are keyed. Processing concurrency can weaken visible order after delivery.
roadmap: Name the ordered entity
Decide whether order matters per account, order, document, or another stable identity.
Choose the partition key
Route related events consistently while measuring potential hot partitions.
Version the event
Include identity and version so consumers can detect duplicates or unexpected sequence gaps.
Bound consumer parallelism
Preserve required per-entity order when processing multiple events concurrently.
Plan partition changes
Understand how repartitioning affects key placement and in-flight work.
Test delayed events
Exercise retries, rebalances, and late completions before claiming business-level ordering.
decisions: Single partition
Use one partition when strict total order and limited throughput fit the requirement.
One ordered stream becomes a throughput and availability boundary.
Entity-keyed partitions
Use entity keys when independent entities can be processed in parallel.
A hot entity can still dominate one partition; uniform key counts are not enough.
Version-aware consumers
Use version checks when late or duplicate events must not regress state.
Gap handling and reconciliation need explicit policy rather than silently discarding every mismatch.
incident: Observe state regression
An older event overwrites a newer business state after parallel processing.
Inspect keys and versions
Compare partition assignment, event versions, and completion order.
Pause the affected consumer
Preserve offsets and evidence while preventing further regression.
Repair processing order
Serialize the required entity boundary or enforce safe version checks.
Rebuild affected state
Replay or reconcile from an authoritative source using the repaired handler.
Test rebalances
Verify correctness across restarts, ownership changes, and delayed workers.
metrics: Partition lag spread
Compare lag across partitions instead of relying only on a total.
One hot or poisoned partition can affect a critical entity while the average looks normal.
Version gaps
Count unexpected entity-version gaps and regressions.
A gap may reflect filtering or retention, so interpret it using the event contract.
Processing skew
Measure completion time by event class and partition.
Delivery order does not guarantee completion order when work runs concurrently.
lab: Create entity events
Generate versioned updates for several synthetic accounts.
Partition by identity
Verify events for one account share the intended ordered boundary.
Delay one update
Make an older update finish after a newer one.
Protect the projection
Use per-entity serialization or validated version handling.
Reassign the consumer
Restart or rebalance while work is in flight.
Audit final versions
Compare the projection with the expected event sequence for every account.
takeaway: State exactly where order is guaranteed: delivery, processing, or the final business effect.

title: A Queue Is Not Infinite Capacity
hook: A queue can hide overload until the delay becomes the outage.
premise: Incoming work must eventually be completed, rejected, expired, or cancelled. Queue capacity and age are part of the user-visible contract.
roadmap: Measure arrival and service
Compare admitted work with sustainable completion rate for each job class.
Bound the backlog
Set capacity or age limits that protect storage and useful completion time.
Apply admission control
Reject, defer, or shed work before accepting obligations the system cannot meet.
Scale the right consumer
Add workers only when the limiting dependency has spare capacity.
Define expiry semantics
Explain what happens to work that is no longer useful after waiting.
Recover without flooding
Drain backlog at a rate that preserves current traffic and downstream health.
decisions: Bounded queue
Use a bounded queue when accepted work must have a predictable resource envelope.
Producers need an explicit rejection or waiting contract when capacity is exhausted.
Durable backlog
Use durable storage when delayed work remains valuable and recovery time is acceptable.
Durability does not make an unbounded delay useful to the customer.
Load shedding
Drop or reject nonessential work when preserving critical service matters more than accepting everything.
The product must define which work is safely discardable and how rejection is reported.
incident: Notice growing age
The queue keeps accepting work while the oldest job becomes increasingly late.
Compare work rates
Measure arrivals, completions, retries, and permanent failures.
Stop accepting impossible work
Apply the documented capacity or age-based admission policy.
Protect downstream systems
Avoid multiplying workers against the same saturated database or API.
Drain selectively
Prioritize useful work and handle expired jobs according to policy.
Verify steady recovery
Confirm backlog age falls while current request objectives remain healthy.
metrics: Oldest job age
Track the age of the oldest useful pending job by work class.
Queue length cannot be interpreted without job duration and arrival distribution.
Net backlog growth
Compare admitted jobs with terminal outcomes over the same interval.
Retries inflate attempts but do not necessarily create useful progress.
Completion within objective
Measure the share of accepted jobs finished before they lose value.
Eventually completing every job can still violate the promised user experience.
lab: Create slow workers
Use synthetic jobs with measured processing durations.
Increase arrival rate
Exceed sustainable completion briefly and observe queue age.
Bound acceptance
Add capacity and deadline-aware admission controls.
Slow the dependency
Show why adding workers may worsen contention instead of fixing throughput.
Exercise recovery
Reduce arrivals and drain while protecting interactive work.
Check every accepted job
Require a completed, failed, expired, or cancelled outcome with clear accounting.
takeaway: A queue buys time only when admission, processing capacity, and expiry are controlled.

title: Dead Letters Need a Runbook
hook: Moving a message to a dead-letter queue does not resolve the customer's problem.
premise: A worker repeatedly fails on a malformed or permanently unsupported event. Separate retryable infrastructure errors from data and business failures.
roadmap: Classify the failure
Separate transient dependency errors from permanent validation or unsupported-schema failures.
Bound retries
Set attempts and delays according to whether another attempt can plausibly help.
Preserve diagnostic context
Keep event identity, schema, and sanitized failure metadata without leaking sensitive payloads.
Quarantine deliberately
Move unrecoverable work to an owned recovery workflow with alerting.
Repair before replay
Fix the handler, transform authorized data, or record a business-approved terminal outcome.
Replay safely
Use original identities and bounded rates so recovery cannot repeat irreversible effects.
decisions: Retry in place
Retry a transient failure when the event remains valid and the attempt budget allows it.
One poison event can block ordered work behind it if the consumer never advances.
Quarantine the event
Isolate permanent failures when the stream can proceed under its ordering contract.
Skipping an event can leave a projection incomplete; make the gap visible.
Stop the partition
Pause processing when continuing without the failed event would violate correctness.
Availability is reduced until repair; ownership and escalation must be explicit.
incident: Find repeated failure
One event consumes many attempts while useful completion stalls.
Inspect the category
Determine whether the failure is transient, schema-related, or a business invariant violation.
Contain the retry loop
Stop unbounded retry traffic without discarding the event.
Assign an owner
Route the quarantined case to a documented recovery responsibility.
Repair and replay
Apply a tested handler fix and replay using the original identity.
Close the business gap
Verify the customer's intended state or record why the operation cannot complete.
metrics: Permanent failure age
Measure how long quarantined events remain unresolved.
An empty main queue can hide a growing dead-letter backlog.
Attempts per event
Track repeated failures by safe error category and schema version.
Large attempt counts are waste when the input cannot succeed without intervention.
Recovery completion
Count cases restored to a valid terminal business state.
Moving bytes between queues is not the same as resolving the original operation.
lab: Create mixed events
Include valid, malformed, and temporarily failing synthetic messages.
Classify retry behavior
Apply different handling for permanent and transient failures.
Preserve the event ID
Keep identity stable through quarantine and repair.
Fix one handler defect
Deploy a local corrected handler and replay a small controlled batch.
Check duplicate safety
Repeat the repaired event and verify a single logical effect.
Audit unresolved cases
Produce a recovery report with owners and explicit remaining gaps.
takeaway: A dead-letter queue is a recovery inbox with an owner, not a graveyard for failed work.

title: Consumers Must Survive Redelivery
hook: Acknowledging a message and committing a business effect are separate failure boundaries.
premise: Assume at-least-once delivery. The consumer must distinguish repeated delivery from a genuinely new business operation.
roadmap: Choose event identity
Use a stable producer identity scoped to the business consumer.
Claim with the effect
Store deduplication state with the business change when they share a transactional database.
Acknowledge after durable work
Avoid acknowledging before the required state is committed.
Handle external effects
Use provider idempotency or reconciliation for effects outside the local transaction.
Plan retention
Keep deduplication history long enough for the supported replay window.
Test both crash sides
Crash before commit and after commit but before acknowledgement.
decisions: Transactional inbox
Use an inbox record and business mutation in one database transaction.
Retention and replay rules must prevent forgotten identities from creating duplicate effects later.
Idempotent state assignment
Use naturally repeatable assignment when applying the same version has no additional effect.
Incrementing counters or sending messages is not equivalent to assigning an absolute versioned state.
Provider idempotency
Use the external service's documented operation-key support for irreversible downstream work.
Your consumer and provider may have different key scopes and retention windows.
incident: Notice duplicate side effects
One event triggers repeated emails, charges, or counter increments.
Compare delivery and operation IDs
Check whether retries changed the logical identity.
Stop irreversible replay
Pause the affected effect while retaining the event stream.
Reconcile authoritative outcomes
Determine which external actions actually completed.
Repair the atomic boundary
Bind deduplication to the business mutation or provider operation key.
Replay crash scenarios
Verify that commit-before-ack redelivery returns the existing result safely.
metrics: Deduplicated deliveries
Count repeated event identities that were safely recognized.
Duplicates are normal for some transports; the metric is not itself a correctness failure.
Repeated business effects
Audit logical operations against their externally visible effects.
Message acknowledgements cannot prove that an effect occurred exactly once.
Deduplication retention
Track oldest retained identities relative to the replay contract.
A replay older than retained history needs an explicit recovery policy.
lab: Build a local consumer
Apply a synthetic event to a database-backed business record.
Deliver it concurrently
Race two workers with the same event identity.
Crash before commit
Verify that replay can safely complete the missing work.
Crash after commit
Lose the acknowledgement and confirm redelivery does not repeat the effect.
Change the payload
Reject conflicting content under the same event identity.
Test old replay
Exercise events near the deduplication-retention boundary.
takeaway: Deduplicate at the business-effect boundary, not merely at message receipt.

title: Replay Is a Production Feature
hook: Replaying yesterday's events can accidentally send yesterday's emails again.
premise: A replay may rebuild a projection, repair a bug, or recover state. Its side-effect policy must be explicit before it touches historical data.
roadmap: Define replay purpose
Separate rebuilding derived state from re-executing external business actions.
Version the handler
Record the schema and transformation version used for the replay.
Isolate the target
Rebuild into a separate projection when comparison and rollback are needed.
Control side effects
Disable or deduplicate irreversible actions according to the approved recovery contract.
Throttle recovery load
Keep replay from starving current traffic or exhausting dependencies.
Verify convergence
Compare rebuilt state and invariants before switching the authoritative read path.
decisions: Full rebuild
Use a full rebuild when the complete event history and compatible interpretation are available.
Retention gaps or changed event meaning can prevent a faithful reconstruction.
Targeted repair
Replay a known affected range or identity set when the defect scope is well established.
A narrow repair can miss hidden dependencies unless the affected set is validated.
Snapshot plus log
Start from a verified snapshot when replaying the full history is too expensive.
The snapshot position and subsequent log continuity must agree exactly.
incident: Find projection divergence
A derived view disagrees with authoritative source or event history.
Bound the affected range
Identify the faulty handler version and event identities involved.
Protect external effects
Prevent recovery from resending notifications or repeating irreversible actions.
Replay into isolation
Build a separate corrected view at a bounded rate.
Compare invariants
Check counts, versions, relationships, and representative business queries.
Switch with a recovery plan
Promote the validated view and retain evidence for rollback or forward repair.
metrics: Replay progress
Track processed position and remaining work in the chosen source history.
A record count does not prove the replay used the correct handler or complete history.
Projection differences
Measure mismatches between rebuilt and expected business state.
Some differences may be the intended bug fix; classify them instead of requiring blind byte equality.
Live traffic impact
Monitor user latency and dependency load while replay runs.
Recovery should not create a second outage by consuming all shared capacity.
lab: Generate an event history
Use synthetic versioned events with a known final state.
Introduce a handler bug
Build one intentionally incorrect local projection.
Fix the transformation
Version the corrected handler and define side-effect policy.
Replay separately
Rebuild a fresh projection without sending external notifications.
Compare results
Assert business invariants and explain every intended difference.
Practice the switch
Promote the repaired view only after a repeatable validation gate.
takeaway: Safe replay needs versioned meaning, side-effect control, and evidence of convergence.
